did_you_know.text: Did you know? Isaiah describes turning to Egypt for help as “going down,” emphasizing that the people rely on horses, chariots, and horsemen instead of looking to the Holy One of Israel and seeking the LORD.
Did you know? The prophet presents the LORD as wise and as one whose words come to pass: he brings disaster on the house of evildoers and on those who rely on workers of iniquity.

Did you know? In this verse, Isaiah draws a sharp contrast between Egypt and the LORD: Egypt is human, and its horses are flesh, while the LORD acts with power free from human weakness. Therefore, both the helper and the one being helped will fall.
Did you know? Isaiah compares the LORD’s standing over Mount Zion to a lion that is not frightened by the noise and crowds of shepherds when it stands over its prey.
Did you know? The LORD’s protection of Jerusalem is described through the image of flying birds: the LORD protects, delivers, passes over, and rescues the city.
Did you know? After describing the LORD’s protection, the prophet speaks directly to the Israelites and calls them to return from the evil path into which they have strayed so deeply.

Did you know? The prophet foresees that on that day the Israelites will reject their idols of silver and gold, emphasizing that these idols are the work of their own hands and have become a source of sin for them.
Did you know? Assyria’s downfall is described as falling by a sword that is not wielded by a human being, while the Assyrian young men will melt away and retreat before the sword.

Did you know? At the end of the chapter, the terror of Assyria’s leaders and the retreat of their stronghold from fear are described; by contrast, the LORD is portrayed as having a fire in Zion and a furnace in Jerusalem.
